name: the National Botanic Gardens
title: Ancient Trees in Dublin's National Botanic Gardens: 7 to Find
meta_description: Dublin's National Botanic Gardens holds a living-fossil dawn redwood, a cultivar-naming Caucasian elm and Ireland's largest Tree of Heaven.
intro: The Dublin Society founded the National Botanic Gardens at Glasnevin in 1795 to teach scientific agriculture, and the collecting habit that started then never stopped. A 2009 heritage survey by the Tree Council of Ireland recorded six of these seven trees as Exceptional Specimen Trees, gathered from three continents across two centuries of curators, all within 200 metres of each other: a dawn redwood grown from the seed that ended the species' presumed extinction in China, an Atlas cedar from a mountain range now losing its wild population to drought, a Caucasian elm so admired a County Offaly nurseryman propagated cuttings from it and sold the result as its own named cultivar, and a bald cypress built for Louisiana swampland doing its best in an Irish flower bed. The seventh and oldest, a formal double avenue of yew, carries the garden's separate Named Trees designation and is said, by tradition rather than record, to have been planted in memory of the essayist Joseph Addison before the gardens themselves existed. Entry is free, every day except Christmas Day, and all seven specimens sit an easy afternoon's walk from each other.
